body:
What is Java?

Java is a high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent language. It uses bytecode and the JVM to hide hardware complexity and make code readable and portable.

JDK, JRE, and JVM

JDK is the toolkit for developers. JRE is the environment to run apps. JVM is the engine that executes bytecode line-by-line using an interpreter/JIT.

Compiler vs Interpreter

The compiler (javac) translates source code to bytecode at once. The interpreter (in JVM) executes that bytecode line-by-line. Java uses both for performance and debugging.
code:
// Step 1: javac App.java -> App.class (Compile)
// Step 2: java App (Interpret)

Platform Independence & Bytecode

Java compiles source to platform-neutral .class files (Bytecode). Any system with a JVM can run these files, making Java 'Write Once, Run Anywhere'.

OOPS Concepts

Encapsulation: Hiding data. Inheritance: Code reuse. Polymorphism: Many shapes. Abstraction: Hiding internal logic.
code:
class Animal { void sound() { } }
class Dog extends Animal { } // Inheritance

Other OOPS: Relationships

Association, Aggregation, and Composition: These define 'has-a' relationships, ranging from loose connections to strict lifecycles.

Java 8 Features

Introduced Lambda Expressions, Stream API, Functional Interfaces, and the Optional class to simplify Java code.

Java 21 Features

Key updates include Virtual Threads (Project Loom), Sequenced Collections, and Record Patterns for better concurrency and syntax.

Memory Management

Heap: Stores objects (Garbage Collected). Stack: Stores method calls and local variables.
code:
Object obj = new Object(); 
// 'obj' on Stack, 'new Object()' on Heap

What is Java?

A high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent language. It uses bytecode and the JVM to ensure code written once runs everywhere while hiding complex hardware details.

JDK, JRE, and JVM

JDK is the full developer kit (Tools + JRE). JRE is the environment to run apps. JVM is the 'mini-computer' that interprets bytecode into machine code.

Compiler vs Interpreter

The compiler (javac) translates all code at once into bytecode. The Interpreter (inside JVM) reads that bytecode line-by-line. Java uses both for a balance of speed and debugging.
code:
// Step 1: javac MyFile.java (Compile to Bytecode)
// Step 2: java MyFile (Interpret/Run via JVM)

While the regular compiler works before execution, the JIT compiler works *during* runtime. It turns frequently used bytecode into native machine code to boost performance.

OOPS: The Four Pillars

Encapsulation: Locking data (Diary). Inheritance: Passing traits (Phone -> SmartPhone). Polymorphism: Many shapes. Abstraction: Hiding complexity (Vending machine).

Java 8 & 21 Features

Java 8: Lambdas and Streams. Java 21: Virtual Threads (Project Loom) for high-performance scaling and Sequenced Collections.

Memory: Heap vs Stack

Heap stores all objects and is cleaned by Garbage Collection. Stack is for short-term method execution and local references. When a method ends, its stack frame is gone.

Kafka, JDBC, and Threads

Kafka: A stream platform for data pipelines. JDBC: Java's way of talking to databases. Threads: Lightweight processes that allow multitasking.
code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Running Thread"));
t.start();

body:
1. Thread in Java

A thread is a lightweight subprocess, the smallest unit of processing. Multithreading allows concurrent execution.

2. JVM (Java Virtual Machine)

Acts as a run-time engine to run Java applications. It loads, verifies, and executes bytecode.

3. Four Pillars of OOPs

The foundation of Java: Inheritance, Polymorphism, Encapsulation, and Abstraction.

4. String vs StringBuilder

String is immutable (constant), while StringBuilder is mutable and efficient for modifications.

5. Interface vs Abstract Class

Interfaces support multiple inheritance. Abstract classes can have constructors and concrete methods.

6. Exception Handling

A mechanism to handle runtime errors using try-catch blocks to maintain flow.

7. JDK vs JRE vs JVM

JDK (Dev Kit) = JRE + Development Tools; JRE (Runtime) = JVM + Libraries.
code:
// Hierarchy:
// [JDK [JRE [JVM]]]

body:
8. Static Keyword

The static keyword belongs to the class rather than instances of the class.

9. Constructor

A special method used to initialize objects; it has no return type and shares the class name.

10. Final Keyword

Used to restrict the user: final variables cannot be changed, and final classes cannot be inherited.
code:
final int SPEED_LIMIT = 90;
final class Vehicle { } // Cannot be extended

body:
11. Array vs ArrayList

Arrays are fixed in size, whereas ArrayList is a dynamic collection.

12. Method Overloading vs Overriding

Overloading is same name, different parameters. Overriding is subclass providing specific logic.
